848.title: Manresa
848.hook: Ignatius spends months in a cave praying and writes notes that become the Spiritual Exercises
848.howItsDone: Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises on retreats, either as a silent retreat away from home or in daily life over a longer stretch, with a guide who meets them regularly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pamplona: a cannonball, a sickbed, and nothing to read but saints. Your line was the cannonball. Did something interrupt your plans? Today the soldier gets up and walks. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

A notebook, in the hand of a man dressed in sackcloth. Before he reached this town he had stopped at the shrine of Our Lady at Montserrat, hung up his sword and dagger there, and given his fine clothes to a beggar. He meant to stay a few days in the small town down the hill. He stayed far longer. He begged for food, let his hair and nails grow, and prayed for hours every day. Tradition points to a cave above the river where he went to pray. And all the while he kept writing in that notebook. The town is Manresa.
screen: `A SWORD LEFT AT MONTSERRAT.` → `A FEW DAYS BECOME A LONG STAY.` → `A NOTEBOOK.`

segments.voice: Manresa was not a peaceful retreat. Ignatius's own account shows four sides of it. First, the dark. He was tormented by scruples, the fear that he hadn't confessed his sins fully. He confessed again and again and found no rest. He says he was tempted to despair. He doesn't hide it. Second, the school. Later he described how God dealt with him at Manresa the way a schoolmaster deals with a child, teaching him one lesson at a time. He wasn't learning from books. He was learning from what happened in him when he prayed. Third, the river. One day, sitting by the river Cardoner, he says the eyes of his understanding began to open. He saw no vision, he says, but understood many things about faith and learning, and everything seemed new. Fourth, the notes. Through all of it, he wrote down what he noticed: what helped, what pulled him under, which way of praying led where. Those notes, reworked over years, became a small handbook called the Spiritual Exercises. It isn't a book to read straight through. It's a set of instructions for someone guiding another person through prayer, step by step. Some readers hear an echo of Mary in the Gospel of Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Ignatius kept them on paper. A soldier who knew nothing about prayer paid close attention, and wrote it down.
screen: `THE DARK: SCRUPLES.` · `GOD AS A SCHOOLMASTER.` · `BY THE RIVER CARDONER.` · `THE NOTES BECOME THE EXERCISES.` · then, large: `PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one thing you noticed in prayer, or in quiet. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, pray for a little while in whatever way you usually do. If you don't, just sit and let your mind be still. Then ask one plain question: what did I notice? A word that stayed. A feeling that came or went. A person who came to mind. Don't judge it. Afterward, write it in one line, on paper or on your phone. The bell holds the time.
Manresa. The Catalan town where Ignatius prayed, struggled and kept a notebook, and where the Spiritual Exercises began.
Your line: notes from a cave. Today, keep the line you wrote, and tonight read it once more. Add a second line if one comes. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: The Society of Jesus (1540)
849.hook: seven friends at Paris become an order, for the greater glory of God
849.howItsDone: Jesuits and students in Jesuit schools often write AMDG, for Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, at the top of their work, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering of everything they'll do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Manresa: scruples, a river, and a notebook that became the Spiritual Exercises. Your line was notes from a cave. Did you read your line again last night? Today the notebook finds friends. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

Ignatius is back in school. In Paris he sits in class, older than the students around him, starting again from the basics. He has decided that to help people, he needs to study. At the university he shares rooms with two younger men, Pierre Favre and Francis Xavier. One by one, a small band of friends gathers around him. On a hill above Paris, at Montmartre, they make vows together. They don't yet know they're founding anything. Today's word is what the world ended up calling them: Jesuit.
screen: `A GROWN MAN LEARNING GRAMMAR.` → `ROOMMATES IN PARIS.` → `VOWS AT MONTMARTRE.`

segments.voice: First, the plan that failed. The friends meant to go to Jerusalem and live where Jesus lived. They waited in Venice for a ship. No pilgrim ship sailed. So they turned to their backup plan: go to Rome and offer themselves to the pope, to be sent wherever he thought best. A failed plan set the shape of everything after. Second, the name. When people asked who they were, they decided to answer: the Company of Jesus, since they had no head but him. In Latin, the Society of Jesus. Pope Paul the Third approved them as a religious order. Jesuit is the everyday name that stuck. Third, the motto, in Latin: Ad maiorem Dei gloriam. For the greater glory of God. Not glory. Greater glory. The question is always comparative: of the choices in front of me, which serves God more? It echoes Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." Fourth, the habit of mind. These weren't monks behind walls. They went where they were sent: schools, ports, courts, slums, mission lands. Ignatius asked them to find God in all things, not only in chapel. Over the centuries the Jesuits have been praised, feared, opposed, even suppressed for a time and then restored. They have their admirers and their critics, inside the Church and out. But the motto hasn't changed. Some Catholic students still write the letters A, M, D, G at the top of their schoolwork.
screen: `THE PLAN THAT FAILED: NO SHIP.` · `THE COMPANY OF JESUS.` · `GREATER GLORY, NOT JUST GLORY.` · `FIND GOD IN ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `AD MAIOREM DEI GLORIAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer today for God's glory. Settle, and breathe. Picture the rest of your day: the work, the conversations, the errands, the boring parts. Hold them all at once. If you pray, you can offer the whole day to God, in your own words or with Paul's: whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God. If you don't pray, choose one thing you'll do today and decide to do it as well as you can, for something bigger than you. The bell holds the time.
Jesuit. A member of the Society of Jesus, the order Ignatius and his friends founded, sent wherever the need is greater, for the greater glory of God.
Your line: for the greater glory. Today, when you face two good options, ask the Jesuit question: which one serves more? Write A M D G at the top of one thing you do. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: Francis Xavier (1506–1552)
850.hook: he baptizes across India and Japan and dies off the coast of China
850.howItsDone: Catholics keep Francis Xavier's feast, and he is honored as a patron of missions; his remains are venerated in Goa, India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesuits: a failed pilgrimage, an offer to the pope, and a motto. Your line was for the greater glory. Which choice served more? Today one of Ignatius's roommates is sent east. Day eight hundred fifty.

The ending comes first. A small island off the coast of China, a hut, a fever, and a man waiting for a boat that never comes. He has a plan to slip into the mainland, where foreigners are forbidden, and he's been told it could cost him his freedom or his life. He's still waiting when he dies. Behind him lie India, the islands of the spice trade, and Japan. He was once a promising young teacher in Paris, rooming with an older student who kept asking him an uncomfortable question. The older student was Ignatius. The young teacher was Francis Xavier.
screen: `AN ISLAND OFF CHINA.` → `A BOAT THAT NEVER COMES.` → `ONCE A TEACHER IN PARIS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Tradition says Ignatius kept repeating one line of the Gospel to his ambitious roommate, from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" Xavier wanted a career. That question slowly turned him around. Second, the sending. When the king of Portugal asked for missionaries for India, another Jesuit was chosen and fell ill. Xavier was sent instead, almost overnight. He never saw Ignatius again. Third, the road. In India he walked the coast, taught children prayers in their own language, and baptized. Then he went on, to the islands, to Japan. In Japan he learned that his ragged clothes made people take him less seriously, not more, and he changed his approach. Then China. He never reached the mainland. Fourth, the letters. Xavier wrote long letters home to his brothers in Europe, and they were copied and read aloud. In one he says he wishes he could run through the universities of Europe shouting to the students about the people waiting for someone to come. It's also true that his travels went by Portuguese ships, inside a trading empire, and that empire's record is a hard one. The Church names him a patron of the missions. His line, if he had one, was always further.
screen: `WHAT DOTH IT PROFIT A MAN?` · `SENT IN ANOTHER MAN'S PLACE.` · `INDIA, THE ISLANDS, JAPAN.` · `LETTERS READ ALOUD IN EUROPE.` · then, large: `ALWAYS FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write to someone far away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone at a distance: another city, another country, or just far from you in the ways that count. Picture their face. What would they be glad to hear from you? Start a message. A few lines are enough. Don't send it yet if you'd rather wait; just begin. If you pray, you can pray for them as you write. If you don't, simply keep them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Francis Xavier. Ignatius's roommate from Paris, sent east to India and Japan, who died on an island off the coast of China, still going further.
Your line: always further. Today, send the message you started, or go one step past where you'd usually stop for someone: one more call, one more mile, one more try. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: Teresa on the road
851.hook: Teresa founds seventeen convents traveling in rough carts
851.carry: a bad night in a bad inn
851.howItsDone: Discalced Carmelite nuns and friars still live by the reform Teresa began, and Catholics read her Foundations, her Life and the Interior Castle as spiritual classics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis Xavier, from a Paris classroom to an island off China. Your line was always further. Did you send that message? Today, another traveler, on rougher roads closer to home. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

The roads of Castile are dirt, and a covered cart lurches along one of them. Inside, a few nuns sit in the heat and the dust, with the curtains drawn. At night they stop at an inn, where the beds are bad, the food is worse, and the other guests are loud. In the morning they climb back in. The nun in charge is often sick, and writing a book about the journey as she goes. Her name is Teresa of Avila, and today we ride with her: Teresa on the road.
screen: `A CART IN THE DUST.` → `A BAD INN, A LOUD NIGHT.` → `A SICK NUN WRITING IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Teresa is known for prayer: the interior castle, the soul as a garden. But she also spent years on the road, founding new convents of her reformed Carmelites, and she wrote it all down in a book called the Foundations. Four things stand out. First, the roads. She describes heat, floods, rivers to cross, and getting lost. She doesn't make it sound holy. She makes it sound tiring. Second, the houses. At one town, she says, the little group arrived in the middle of the night, set up an altar, and had Mass at dawn. Only in daylight did she see how much the walls were crumbling. She was dismayed, and stayed. Third, the inn. In her Way of Perfection, Teresa compares this life, seen from heaven, to one bad night in a bad inn. It's a joke, and it isn't. Uncomfortable, yes. But it's one night, and morning comes. Some readers hear the same idea in the Letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we have not here a lasting city, but we seek one that is to come." Fourth, the humor. Teresa is funny on the page. She grumbles, laughs at herself, and admits when she's scared. People still tell a story of her falling from a cart into a river and complaining to God about how he treats his friends. That one comes from stories told about her, not from her own books. But it sounds like her. Holiness, in her hands, was not a calm road. It was a cart that kept moving.
screen: `THE FOUNDATIONS: A TRAVEL BOOK.` · `A HOUSE WITH CRUMBLING WALLS.` · `ONE BAD NIGHT IN A BAD INN.` · `FUNNY, SCARED, STILL GOING.` · then, large: `WE HAVE NOT HERE A LASTING CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep going on a hard road. Settle, and breathe. Name one hard stretch you're on right now: a job, a recovery, a relationship, a long wait. Picture it as a road, with you in the cart. Don't pretend it's comfortable. Just ask: what's the next mile? Only the next one. If you pray, you can hand the road to God, the way Teresa did, complaints and all. If you don't, simply breathe with it, and let the morning be coming. The bell holds the time.
Teresa on the road. The mystic of Avila, traveling by cart to found convents, who called this life one bad night in a bad inn, and kept going.
Your line: a bad night in a bad inn. Today, when something goes badly, say it to yourself, with a smile if you can, and then take the next mile. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

852.title: Philip Neri (1515–1595)
852.hook: the laughing saint of Rome, who taught with jokes and music
852.howItsDone: Oratorian communities in cities around the world still hold gatherings of prayer, talk and music in Philip Neri's style, and the priests live together without vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa in her cart, laughing at herself on rough roads. Your line was a bad night in a bad inn. Did you get to use it? Today, a saint remembered for his laughter. Day eight hundred fifty-two.
screen: `A BAD NIGHT IN A BAD INN.`

segments.voice: An upstairs room in Rome, crowded in the afternoon. Young men from the shops and the banks, a few priests, some students, sitting on benches. Someone reads a page from a saint's life. A priest in a worn cassock asks what they made of it, and the talk goes around the room. Then someone sings. Then more talk, and somebody laughs. Nobody here is a monk. Nobody took a vow to come. The priest is Philip Neri, and the room gave its name to today's word: Oratory.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM IN ROME.` → `A READING, A QUESTION, A SONG.` → `NOBODY TOOK A VOW.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Philip came to Rome from Florence as a young layman and spent years praying in churches and, tradition says, in the catacombs by night, and talking with anyone in the streets. He became a priest later, and he never stopped talking with people. Second, the room. An oratory is a place of prayer, smaller than a church. Philip's gatherings in his room grew so large they needed one, and the group that ran them became the Congregation of the Oratory: priests living together without vows, held only by charity. Third, the music. Philip wanted the meetings to be something people looked forward to. Musicians sang hymns and spiritual songs in the language of the street, so a shopkeeper could follow along. Fourth, the jokes. Tradition remembers Philip as the laughing saint. Stories say he shaved half his beard, or read silly books in front of important visitors, so nobody would take him for holy. One story has a woman confess to gossip. He tells her to pluck a chicken while walking through the streets, then go back and gather every feather. She can't, of course. That, he says, is what gossip is like. Whether every story happened, the laughter was the point. Philip used it to keep himself humble and to keep sadness from settling in. Some readers hear his spirit in a line from Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." For Philip, joy was not a reward for being holy. It was part of the road.
screen: `A LAYMAN IN THE STREETS OF ROME.` · `A ROOM BECOMES AN ORATORY.` · `SONGS IN THE STREET'S LANGUAGE.` · `HALF A BEARD, AND THE FEATHERS.` · then, large: `REJOICE IN THE LORD ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make someone laugh. Settle, and breathe. Smile a little, even if it feels silly. Now think of someone who could use a lighter day. What makes them laugh? A memory you share. A ridiculous photo. A joke that's on you, not on anyone else. Choose one, and plan when you'll send or say it. If you pray, you can thank God for laughter, and for them. If you don't, simply enjoy the thought of their face when it lands. The bell holds the time.
Oratory. A place of prayer, and the name of Philip Neri's community in Rome, born from crowded afternoons of reading, talk and music.
Your line: holy joy. Today, send the joke, or say it. And when you catch yourself taking yourself too seriously, remember half a beard. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

853.title: Charles Borromeo (1538–1584)
853.hook: a rich reforming bishop who stayed in Milan through the plague
853.howItsDone: Catholics honor Charles Borromeo as a patron of bishops, seminarians and catechists, and seminaries named for him still train priests.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip Neri, half a beard and a room full of songs. Your line was holy joy. Who laughed? Today, a very different saint: serious, thin, and stubborn about one thing. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Plague in Milan. Shops shut, streets empty, carts collecting the dead. Those who can afford to leave the city are leaving, and some of the officials go with them. One carriage is going the other way. The archbishop, who had been away, comes back in. He's from a wealthy, powerful family, and the nephew of a pope. He could have stayed safely away. Instead he walks the streets, visits the sick, and organizes food and care. His name is Charles Borromeo.
screen: `PLAGUE IN MILAN.` → `THE RICH ARE LEAVING.` → `ONE CARRIAGE COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the privilege. Charles was made a cardinal very young, because his uncle was the pope. That's exactly the kind of favoritism reformers complained about. He could have enjoyed it. Instead he worked hard in Rome to help bring the Council of Trent to its close. Second, the reform. The council told bishops to live in their own dioceses and care for their people. That sounds obvious, but the council was answering a real problem: bishops who lived far away and simply drew the income. Charles moved to Milan and stayed there. He visited parishes, opened seminaries to train priests, and pared down his own household. Not everyone loved him for it. Some resisted his reforms, and one group even tried to have him killed. Third, the plague. When the sickness came, he stayed and served. Tradition says he gave away his own goods, even his household hangings, to clothe the poor, and led processions of prayer through the city barefoot. Fourth, the shepherd. Some readers see in him Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." In the same chapter Jesus describes the hired hand who sees the wolf coming and runs. The difference isn't courage, the chapter suggests. It's whose sheep they are. Charles treated Milan as his own. The rich young cardinal is remembered for something simple. He stayed.
screen: `A CARDINAL BY FAVORITISM.` · `REFORM: LIVE WITH YOUR PEOPLE.` · `THE PLAGUE, AND THE BARE FEET.` · `THE SHEPHERD AND THE HIRED HAND.` · then, large: `THE GOOD SHEPHERD GIVETH HIS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay when it's hard. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place, a person, or a task you'd like to escape right now. A tense family, a difficult job, a friend who's struggling, a project gone stale. Don't decide anything big. Just notice the pull to leave. Then ask: is there one small way to stay a little longer, today, with care? If you pray, you can ask for the strength to stay. If you don't, just breathe, and stay with the question. The bell holds the time.
Charles Borromeo. The reforming archbishop of Milan, a pope's nephew from a rich family who lived with his people and stayed with them through the plague.
Your line: he stayed. Today, choose one hard thing you won't walk away from yet. Give it one more hour, one more visit, or one more patient conversation. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

854.title: Peter Canisius (1521–1597)
854.hook: he wrote simple catechisms for the people of Germany
854.howItsDone: Catholic parishes run catechism classes for children and adults preparing for the sacraments, and the Church publishes catechisms, from short ones for families to the full Catechism of the Catholic Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles Borromeo came back into a city with plague. Your line was he stayed. What did you stay with? This week took us from a cave at Manresa, to the Jesuits, Xavier, Teresa's cart, Philip's laughter and Milan. Today, a man with a pen. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

What is a Christian? A child should be able to answer that. So should a farmer, a baker, a soldier. But in German lands, in a century of fierce argument about faith, the shouting could drown out the explaining. A Jesuit from the Netherlands, Peter Canisius, decided to try something modest. Short questions. Short answers. A little book a family could keep by the fire, and a child could learn by heart. Today's word is that little book: catechism.
screen: `WHAT IS A CHRISTIAN?` → `MORE SHOUTING THAN EXPLAINING.` → `A LITTLE BOOK BY THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: First, the form. A catechism teaches by question and answer. Someone asks, someone answers, and the answer is short enough to remember. It's how a parent teaches a child, and it's very old. Canisius didn't invent it. He made it work for his age. Second, the sizes. He wrote a longer catechism for students and teachers, and a small one for children and ordinary people. Same faith, different doorways. He knew that a farmer and a professor need different books. Third, the tone. This was the age of the Reformation, an age of bitter pamphlets on both sides. In his letters, Canisius urged fellow Catholics toward patience and charity with those who disagreed, and warned that harshness drove people further away. His catechisms set out what the Church teaches, plainly, more than they attack anyone. Fourth, the root. Some readers connect teaching the faith with a line in the First Letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." A reason, not a lecture. Canisius traveled constantly, preached, founded schools, and wrote. His small books were printed again and again. The Church later named him a Doctor of the Church. But his real gift was simple: he trusted that a hard truth could be said in simple words.
screen: `QUESTION AND ANSWER.` · `A BIG BOOK AND A SMALL ONE.` · `PATIENCE, NOT HARSHNESS.` · `A REASON FOR THE HOPE.` · then, large: `SIMPLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain your faith simply, or whatever you hold most deeply. Settle, and breathe. Imagine a child, or a curious friend, asking you one honest question: what do you believe, and why? Don't reach for big words. Try to answer in two or three plain sentences, the way Canisius would have written it. If you're still searching, say that simply too; that's an honest answer. If you pray, you can ask for the right words. The bell holds the time.
Catechism. A book that teaches the faith by short questions and answers, like the ones Peter Canisius wrote for scholars and for children.
Your line: simple words. Today, when you explain anything, a task, a feeling, an idea, try saying it in the plainest words you have, and see if it lands better. Day eight hundred fifty-four.
